lesson_title: The Magnet You Can Switch Off
hook_text: A scrapyard crane lifts a whole car with a magnet, then just lets it go. How do you switch a magnet off?
clip_script: A scrapyard crane swings a big metal disc over a pile of old cars. The operator presses a button and a car leaps up and sticks. Swing, release, crash. There is no ordinary magnet in that disc, just a coil of copper wire wrapped around iron. In 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed a compass needle twitch near a wire whenever he switched the current on. Current makes magnetism. Coil the wire and the effect adds up; put soft iron inside and it gets massively stronger. Switch off the current and the magnet vanishes. That is an electromagnet, and it is in doorbells, speakers, motors and the locks on security gates. And current does two more things: it heats every wire it flows through, which is how your kettle works and why a fuse melts, and it splits liquids apart, which is how taps get their shiny chrome coat.
visual_style: A whiteboard crane lifting a car, then a zoom into a coil around an iron core with field lines appearing when the switch closes, then quick sketches of a glowing element and a bubbling electrolysis cell.
pacing: A dramatic lift and drop, a clear explanation, then a quick tour of the other two effects.
